posts.title: 2027 dates: three nights from 30 July, and a 70th summer
posts.excerpt: The 70th Minase River Hanabi runs from Friday 30 July to Sunday 1 August 2027: three nights, eighteen thousand shells, and passes on sale on 1 May.
posts.content:
The committee met on Tuesday evening in the hall above the shopping street, and it took less than an hour: the 70th Minase River Hanabi will run for three nights, from Friday 30 July to Sunday 1 August 2027.

It is the first time since 2011 that we have added anything to the festival. Friday becomes a full opening night with taiko and four thousand shells; Saturday stays the finale; Sunday keeps its lanterns.

What changes

  • Eighteen thousand shells over three nights, up from fifteen thousand
  • The Lantern Stage moves deeper into Tenjin Park, away from the houses on the south bank
  • A third launch barge, so the starmine finale can cross the whole river
  • The accessible deck doubles in size and gets its own toilets

What does not

The riverbank stays free. It has been free since two fishing boats fired three hundred shells in 1958, and it will be free in 2058. Passes pay for the stages, the stewards and the clean-up, never for the view.

Passes go on sale on 1 May 2027 at 10:00. Readers of The Fuse, our newsletter, will hear a week before everyone else, together with the full lineup.

posts.title: The first twelve acts for the River Stage and the Lantern Stage
posts.excerpt: Kingyo Sound System close Saturday, The Paper Lanterns open the River Stage on Friday, and Hotaru Strings play the lanterns down the river on Sunday.
posts.content:
Mina Sorano has been booking the stages since 2014, and she says this is the earliest she has ever been able to name a headliner. Here are the first twelve of forty-two acts.

The three nights, three headliners

The Paper Lanterns close Friday on the River Stage, ten minutes after the last shell. Kingyo Sound System, the festival dub collective from the coast, play Saturday after the finale and until the very end. On Sunday Hotaru Strings, twelve players on the Tenjin steps, play while three thousand lanterns go down the river.

We booked the bands who would still play if the speakers failed.

Mina Sorano · music programmer

And the town

As every year, a third of the lineup lives within cycling distance: the Minase High School Wind Band, the Kawabe Choir, Little Komainu, and, opening the whole festival, Asagi River Taiko. The full list and the timetable are on the program page and will grow through the spring.

posts.title: Inside the Kurata workshop: how a 30-inch shell is packed
posts.excerpt: Two weeks, four hundred stars and one fuse: Tetsuo Kurata shows how the biggest shell of the festival is made, by hand, twenty minutes upriver.
posts.content:
The Kurata workshop is three low sheds in a cedar wood twenty minutes upriver from Minase, a long way from the nearest house, as the law requires. Tetsuo Kurata is the third generation to work there. His grandfather made signal flares for fishing boats; in 1974 the family packed its first festival shells.

A sphere of stars

A Japanese shell is round, and it bursts round. Inside its paper casing are rings of hoshi, stars: small pellets of colour, each rolled by hand in layers like a sweet, so that a single star can change from orange to marigold to magenta as it burns. The middle is filled with the burst charge, and a time fuse runs in from the top.

The 30-inch shell for Saturday's finale holds about four hundred stars in three rings. Packing it takes two weeks; pasting the layers of paper around it, and letting each one dry, takes most of that time.

If one star is out of place, the whole sky sees it.

Tetsuo Kurata

Four seconds

At 20:55 on Saturday 31 July it will be lifted by crane onto the middle barge, and fired from a steel mortar as tall as a person. It climbs for eleven seconds and opens five hundred metres wide. Then it is gone, and the workshop starts on next year's.

posts.title: 2026 in numbers: 212,000 visitors and the cleanest morning yet
posts.excerpt: The 69th festival in figures, from the visitors on the banks to the bags of rubbish the volunteers did not need to fill.
posts.content:
The counting is done. Here is the 69th Minase River Hanabi in numbers, with thanks to everyone who came, and everyone who took their rubbish home.

  • 212,000 visitors over two nights, in a town of nine thousand
  • 15,000 shells, and one 30-inch shell that opened perfectly
  • 38 acts on two stages, 196 food and game stalls
  • 4,700 extra seats on the Asagi Line on Saturday alone
  • 41 fewer bags of rubbish than in 2025, and a river clean by 06:50

The number we are proudest of is the last one. At dawn on Sunday, two hundred volunteers walked the 1.2 km of bank. For the first time they finished before seven.

The numbers we want to improve: the queue at the station after the finale (forty minutes at worst), and the toilets on the south bank. Both are on the list for 2027.

posts.title: Volunteer crews for 2027: sign up for a night or a morning
posts.excerpt: Six hundred people in orange make the festival work. Night crews, morning crews and the lantern table are all open for 2027.
posts.content:
The festival has one paid office of three people. Everything else, from the gates to the lantern table to the morning clean-up, is done by about six hundred volunteers in orange shirts. Kenta Mizushima, who leads them, is looking for the 2027 crews.

The crews

  • Night crews — gates, stewarding and the water points, 16:00 to 23:00
  • Morning crews — the riverbank clean-up, 05:30 to 07:30, breakfast included
  • Lantern table — helping visitors write and fold lanterns on Sunday
  • Kids' corner — name bands and the lost-children tent

You can sign up for a single shift. Everyone gets an orange festival shirt, a meal, and on Saturday a place on the volunteers' bank right opposite the middle barge.

Write to the volunteers' desk with the nights you can do, and we will be in touch in the spring.

posts.title: Lantern Float Night: how a paper lantern gets to the sea
posts.excerpt: Three thousand lanterns go down the Asagi after the last shell on Sunday. Where they go next is a small piece of town logistics.
posts.content:
Lantern Float Night started in 2011, after a hard spring, as a quiet third evening: anyone could write a name or a wish on a paper lantern and float it down the river after the last shell. Fifteen years later it is the night many people in town like best.

Where they go

Every lantern is made of paper and a wooden base, with a small LED candle instead of a flame. Six hundred metres downriver, past Kitano Bridge, the rowing club waits in boats with long nets. Every lantern is caught, the candles are collected for next year, and the paper is composted by the shrine.

Lantern writing opens at 16:00 at the table in Tenjin Park. The lanterns are free; a donation box pays for the next year's paper.

posts.title: A first-timer's kit: a mat, a fan and a cooling towel
posts.excerpt: Everything worth bringing to your first night on the riverbank, and the few things worth leaving at home.
posts.content:
Every year thousands of people come to the river for the first time. Here is what the committee packs, after seventy summers of practice.

Bring

  • A mat or a cushion: the levee grass is damp after sunset
  • A round fan and a cooling towel, because July evenings stay warm
  • Water, and a bag for your rubbish
  • Ear defenders for small children
  • A charged phone with the festival map saved

Leave at home

  • Glass bottles, barbecues and camping stoves
  • Drones: the air over the river is closed all day
  • Big umbrellas: they block the view behind you

And if you want to dress for it, several shops on the shopping street rent yukata on festival days, and will tie your obi for you. Book a slot early; they fill up by lunchtime.

posts.title: Asagi River Taiko will lead the opening procession
posts.excerpt: Forty drummers from the town's taiko group will walk the festival down to the water on Friday 30 July.
posts.content:
For the new opening night, the festival will start the old way: with drums. At 18:30 on Friday 30 July, the forty drummers of Asagi River Taiko will set off from Minase Station and walk the visitors down Kawabe-dori to the river.

The group was founded in 1986 by the fire brigade, and practises twice a week in the school gym. Its youngest member is nine; its oldest, seventy-four, was a boy on the bank at the very first festival in 1958.

You do not hear the big drum. You feel it in your ribs.

Asagi River Taiko

The procession takes about twenty minutes. Walk with it, or wait on Hotaru Bridge, where the drummers stop to play before the first shell goes up.
